result: Lanceolate complexes at three hair follicle types (guard, awl/auchene, zigzag) are mechanosensory end organs formed by unique combinations of LTMRs (Aβ RA-, Aδ-, C-LTMRs) and terminal Schwann cells (TSCs). Each hair follicle type is innervated by a specific combination of LTMR subtypes.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C15, and C26-C29 establish the basic anatomical organization of lanceolate complexes. These claims are well-supported by prior literature (cited work), immunostaining data (Figure 1), and are consistent with established knowledge about hair follicle innervation patterns in mice.

result: Background information on hair follicle biology: hair follicles cover >90% of mammalian body surface, have multiple functions (thermoregulation, perspiration, mechanosensation), and exist as three subtypes in mouse back skin with distinct developmental timing and morphological features.
evaluation: Claims C11-C25 provide established background knowledge about hair follicle biology, development, and classification. These are well-documented facts from prior literature (appropriately cited) and serve as context for the experimental work.

result: Genetic tools for visualizing LTMR subtypes: C-LTMRs are visualized in ThCreER;Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice, Aδ-LTMRs in TrkB(Nrtk2)tauEGFP mice, and Aβ RA-LTMRs in Npy2r-GFP mice.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 describe established genetic labeling methods from prior work (Li et al., 2011). These tools are validated and their use is demonstrated in Figure 1, providing reliable visualization of distinct LTMR subtypes.

result: All three LTMR subtypes (C-, Aδ-, Aβ RA-LTMRs) form morphologically similar longitudinal lanceolate endings at hair follicles, with TSC cell bodies at the base and finger-shaped processes extending toward the skin surface, encasing individual LTMR endings.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 describe the basic morphology of lanceolate complexes demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 1. The data clearly show S100+ TSCs associated with each LTMR subtype with the described morphological features. This is consistent with prior EM studies cited by the authors.

result: Guard hair follicles have significantly more TSCs (13.4±1.3) than awl/auchene (5.0±0.2) or zigzag (3.7±0.1) follicles. TSC density is comparable between zigzag and awl/auchene follicles but significantly higher at guard hairs.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 present quantitative data from Figure 2C-D with appropriate statistical analysis (p-values reported). Sample sizes appear adequate (n=5-64 follicles), and the measurements are straightforward counts normalized by follicle circumference. The statistical comparisons support the stated conclusions.

result: TSC morphology differs between hair follicle types: TSCs at zigzag and awl/auchene follicles have comparable morphologies, while guard hair TSCs have smaller cell bodies (50.0±3.5 μm²) and considerably longer processes (27.3±1.1 μm) compared to the other types.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by quantitative morphometric analysis in Figure 2H-J using sparse genetic labeling (Plp1CreER;Rosa26YFP). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.05 or p<0.001), and sample sizes (n=10-25 follicles) are reasonable for morphometric analysis.

result: TSC processes at individual hair follicles are tiled (non-overlapping), as demonstrated by multicolor genetic labeling showing adjacent TSCs with distinct fluorescent reporters exhibit non-overlapping processes.
evaluation: Claims C45 and C5 are supported by elegant multicolor labeling experiments using Plp1CreER;Rosa26-Confetti mice (Figure 3A,B). The authors report 100% of examined follicles (109 non-guard, 23 guard) showed tiled TSC arrangements, providing strong quantitative support.

result: Individual TSCs host axonal endings of more than one LTMR subtype, as demonstrated by triple labeling showing C-LTMR and Aδ-LTMR endings associated with processes of the same TSC.
evaluation: Claims C46 and C6 are supported by triple-labeling experiments (ThCreER;Rosa26tdTomato;TrkBtauEGFP mice) shown in Figure 3C,C′ and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The imaging clearly demonstrates interdigitated endings from different LTMR subtypes associated with the same TSC process, replicated across multiple animals.

result: At guard hair follicles, Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate endings have a distinctive ultrastructure: each axonal terminal is encased by TSC processes on three sides (triangular cross-section), contains densely packed mitochondria, and forms small protrusions aligned against the hair follicle basal lamina.
evaluation: Claims C47-C51 describe ultrastructural features observed by transmission EM (Figure 4A,B,B′). The EM images clearly show the described triangular arrangement, mitochondrial density, and axonal protrusions. The observations are consistent across multiple sections from multiple animals (n=2 mice, multiple measurements).

result: At awl/auchene and zigzag follicles, lanceolate endings have distinct ultrastructure: axonal terminals are encased on two sides (spindle-shaped cross-sections), adjacent endings often share TSC processes, and axons show heterogeneous mitochondrial content (some with many, others with few mitochondria).
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by EM analysis (Figure 4C,D, Figure 5, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). The heterogeneity in mitochondrial content is quantified and shown to be consistent across serial sections spanning >3 μm. Quantitative measurements of TSC process width, axon area, and gap sizes are provided with appropriate sample sizes.

result: TrkA signaling is required for development of C-LTMR and Aβ RA-LTMR endings but not Aδ-LTMR endings. In Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice, C-LTMRs and Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate endings are lost while Aδ-LTMR endings remain intact. This allows identification of LTMR subtypes by mitochondrial content: C-LTMRs have few mitochondria, while Aδ- and Aβ RA-LTMRs have abundant mitochondria.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by genetic ablation experiments (Figure 6) combined with EM analysis. The loss of specific LTMR subtypes is demonstrated by immunostaining (Figure 6A-C), and the correlation with mitochondrial content is shown by EM comparison of control vs. TrkA mutant tissue (Figure 6D,E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B). The logic is sound, though it relies on the assumption stated in C61 that TrkA mutation doesn't affect mitochondrial density in Aδ-LTMRs.

result: Lanceolate endings contain numerous small vesicles (likely glutamate-containing) and TSC processes have many pinocytotic vesicles on inner and outer surfaces, which may mediate neuron-glia communication and regulate lanceolate complex assembly/maintenance.
evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by EM observations (Figure 7A-C). However, C63 is speculative—the authors cite recent studies suggesting these are glutamate vesicles but provide no direct evidence. The functional interpretation about communication and regulation is reasonable speculation based on cited work but not directly tested in this study.

result: Prominent hemidesmosomes on hair follicle epithelial cells give rise to ~100 nm filament-like structures that traverse the basal lamina and appear to contact both LTMR axonal endings and TSC processes, potentially serving as mechanical tethers for mechanotransduction.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 describe novel ultrastructural observations from tannic acid-treated EM specimens (Figure 7D-G). The structures are clearly visible in the EM images, and measurements of filament length (~100 nm) are provided. The comparison to anchoring filaments/fibrils is appropriate given the cited literature. However, the functional interpretation about mechanotransduction, while plausible, is speculative.

result: Genetic ablation of TSCs leads to complete loss of longitudinal lanceolate endings and partial loss of circumferential endings at hair follicles, indicating that LTMR axon terminals retract from hair follicles following TSC ablation.
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 and C7 are supported by TSC ablation experiments using Plp1CreER;Rosa26hDTR mice treated with diphtheria toxin (Figure 8). The loss of longitudinal endings is complete (100% of TSC-depleted follicles) and clearly demonstrated by immunostaining for multiple axonal markers (Tuj1, NFH, CGRP). The interpretation that axons retract is reasonable given the data.

result: Following skin denervation in adult mice, TSCs remain intact and associated with hair follicles for at least 44 days, maintaining both location and structural integrity. In contrast, other Schwann cell types (circumferential and myelinating) degenerate. TSC numbers remain comparable to controls even 5 weeks post-denervation.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76, C8, and C86 are supported by denervation experiments (Figure 9). Multiple visualization methods (S100 immunostaining, genetic labeling with Plp1CreER;Rosa26GCaMP3) consistently show TSC persistence. Quantification (Figure 9G) demonstrates no significant change in TSC numbers at guard or non-guard follicles (n=3 animals). The contrast with other Schwann cell types strengthens the conclusion about TSC-specific stability.

result: Following denervation, hair follicles undergo re-innervation with ~70% of skin re-innervated by 33 days and ~90% of follicles showing some re-innervation by 5 weeks. Guard hairs recover faster than non-guard follicles. Importantly, LTMR subtype-hair follicle specificity is largely preserved during regeneration, as Aβ RA-LTMRs (Npy2r-GFP+) re-innervate guard and awl/auchene but not zigzag follicles, and TSCs become re-associated with regenerated axons.
evaluation: Claims C77-C83, C9, and C10 are supported by time-course re-innervation experiments (Figure 10). The progression of re-innervation is documented at multiple time points (7, 21, 28, 33, 35, 83 days). Critically, the specificity of re-innervation is demonstrated using Npy2r-GFP mice (Figure 10G,H), showing that Aβ RA-LTMRs re-establish their original innervation pattern. This is strong evidence for TSC-dependent guidance of regenerating axons.

result: The unique physiological properties and adaptation rates of different LTMR subtypes at awl/auchene and zigzag follicles are due to intrinsic neuronal differences rather than unique end organ morphologies, since different LTMR subtypes share similar lanceolate ending morphologies and can associate with the same TSCs.
evaluation: Claim C84 is a major interpretive conclusion stated in the Discussion. It is well-supported by the collective findings that: (1) different LTMR subtypes have morphologically similar lanceolate endings (C33), (2) they share the same TSCs (C46), and (3) their ultrastructural properties at awl/auchene and zigzag follicles are comparable (C52-C56). This challenges previous assumptions about end organ morphology determining LTMR properties.

result: TSCs serve as anchors or scaffolds that maintain LTMR endings and lanceolate complex structure and integrity, as demonstrated by the loss of LTMR endings following TSC ablation and the persistence of TSCs following denervation.
evaluation: Claim C85 is a major conclusion supported by the complementary ablation (C68-C71) and denervation (C72-C76) experiments. The asymmetric dependency (LTMRs require TSCs, but TSCs don't require LTMRs in adults) is clearly demonstrated. This is a well-supported mechanistic insight into lanceolate complex maintenance.
